# Overview {visibility="hidden"}

# Two-species models



# Community occupancy models

## Community occupancy model

::: {.content-card}
::: {.lead}
Species may go undetected for a couple reason:
:::

::: {.incremental}
1. They are rare and are not present in our sample.
2. They are present in our sample but are cryptic.
:::
:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}
Older methods like rarefaction attempt to address the first issue but not the second. 
:::

::: {.fragment}
We have to address both issues to obtain unbiased estimates of community parameters like species richness. 
:::



## Community occupancy model

::: {style='font-size: 75%;'}
Occupancy of species $i$ present at site $j$:

$$
  z_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\psi_i)
$$

::: {.fragment}
Detection data for species $i$ at site $j$ on occasion $k$:

$$
  y_{ijk} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(z_{ij} \times p_i)
$$
:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}
Species-specific parameters can be modeled as functions of covariates and/or regarded as random effects. Here's an example without covariates:

$$
  \mathrm{logit}(\psi_i) \sim \mathrm{Norm}(\mu_{\psi}, \sigma^2_{\psi})
$$

$$
  \mathrm{logit}(p_i) \sim \mathrm{Norm}(\mu_{p}, \sigma^2_{p})
$$

:::
:::



## Species richness

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}
What do we do if we don't know how many species are in the community?

::: {.content-card}

Two options:

::: {.fragment}
1. Model only the species that were in the sample.
    * This won't let you estimate actual richness, but it will let you account for species (in the sample) that were present but not detected at some sites.
:::

::: {.fragment}
2. Estimate the number of species that were *not* detected in the sample.
    * This can be accomplished using data augmentation.
    * Ideally, we would use some sort of "species checklist" to focus on species that [could have been present]{.callout--caution}. 
:::

:::

:::



## Simulation without covariates

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}
```{r}
#| label: sim-mso-nocov
#| code-line-numbers: "1-3|5-9|11-14|16-24"

R <- 50    # n_species
J <- 40    # n_sites
K <- 3     # n_visits

## Occupancy as logit-normal random effects 
set.seed(34020)
mu_logit_psi <- -2
sd_logit_psi <- 1
psi <- plogis(rnorm(n=R, mean=mu_logit_psi, sd=sd_logit_psi))

## Detection prob as logit-normal random effects
mu_logit_p <- -1
sd_logit_p <- 0.5
p <- plogis(rnorm(n=R, mean=mu_logit_p, sd=sd_logit_p))

## Occupancy and data
z <- matrix(NA, nrow=R, ncol=J) # latent occupancy state for species i at site j
yall <- array(NA, dim=c(R,J,K)) # Data (except we don't know spp that weren't detected)
for(i in 1:R) {
  z[i,] <- rbinom(n=J, size=1, prob=psi[i])
  for(j in 1:J) {
    yall[i,j,] <- rbinom(n=K, size=1, prob=z[i,j]*p[i])
  }
}
```
:::



## Simulation without covariates


::: {style='font-size: 70%;'}

```{r, echo=-1}
#| label: psi-re
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(psi, xlab="Species-level occupancy (psi)", cex.lab=1.5, main="")
hist(p, xlab="Species-level detection probability (p)", cex.lab=1.5, main="")
```
:::



## Simulation without covariates


::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}

Some species were not detected, and thus can't be part of the dataset. 

```{r}
#| label: missed-spp
detected <- rowSums(yall)>0
table(detected)
```

We discard them like so:
```{r}
y <- yall[detected,,] # Discard species that weren't detected
```

:::


## JAGS model ignoring missed species


```{r}
#| label: comm-occ-knownR
#| echo: false
library(jagsUI); library(coda)
writeLines(readLines("comm-occ-knownR.jag"))
```


## JAGS model ignoring missed species

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: jags-fit-knownR
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: '50%'
#| fig-align: 'center'
#| results: hide
#| cache: true
library(jagsUI); library(coda)
jd_fixedR <- list(y=y, n_species=nrow(y), n_sites=ncol(y), n_occasions=dim(y)[3])
jp_fixedR <- c("mu_logit_psi", "sd_logit_psi", "mu_logit_p", "sd_logit_p")
ji_fixedR <- function() list(mu_logit_psi=rnorm(1), sd_logit_psi=rexp(1),
                             mu_logit_p=rnorm(1), sd_logit_p=rexp(1),
                             z=matrix(1, nrow=nrow(y), ncol=ncol(y)))

post_fixedR <- jags.basic(data=jd_fixedR, inits=ji_fixedR, parameters.to.save=jp_fixedR,
                          model.file="comm-occ-knownR.jag", n.chains=1, n.iter=2000)

```
:::


## JAGS model ignoring missed species


::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: jags-mcmc-fixedR-1
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
plot(post_fixedR[,c("mu_logit_p", "mu_logit_psi")])
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: jags-mcmc-fixedR-2
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
plot(post_fixedR[,c("sd_logit_p", "sd_logit_psi")])
```
:::

:::

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}
<center>
We shouldn't be surprised by upward bias in estimation of occupancy and detection parameters because we're ignoring species with low detection/occupancy probabilities.
</center>
:::



## Expanding the model to estimate richness

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}
<br>
We can use data augmentation to infer how many species were missed, and thus estimate the size of the entire community. 

::: {.fragment}
<br>

Here's the expanded part of the model:

$$
w_i \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\Omega) \\
z_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Bern}(w_i \times \psi_{i})
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
where $w_i$ indicates if species $i$ is part of the community such that $R=\sum_{i=1}^M w_i$, and the expected number of species in the community is $E(R)=M \Omega$.
:::

:::

## JAGS model estimating richness


```{r}
#| label: comm-occ-unknownR
#| echo: false
writeLines(readLines("comm-occ-unknownR.jag"))
```



## JAGS model estimating richness

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}

<br>

```{r echo=1:13}
#| label: jags-fit-unknownR
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: '40%'
#| fig-align: 'center'
#| results: hide
#| cache: true
M <- 100                       # Augment to M=100 possible species
y_aug <- array(0, c(M,J,K))
y_aug[1:nrow(y),,] <- y        # Insert observed data

jd_unknownR <- list(y=y_aug, M=M, n_sites=ncol(y), n_occasions=dim(y)[3])
jp_unknownR <- c("mu_logit_psi", "sd_logit_psi", "mu_logit_p", "sd_logit_p", "R")
ji_unknownR <- function() list(mu_logit_psi=rnorm(1), sd_logit_psi=0.1,
                               mu_logit_p=rnorm(1), sd_logit_p=0.1,
                               w=rep(1, M), z=matrix(1, nrow=M, ncol=ncol(y)))

post_unknownR <- jags.basic(data=jd_unknownR, inits=ji_unknownR,
                            parameters.to.save=jp_unknownR,
                            model.file="comm-occ-unknownR.jag", n.chains=1, n.iter=5000)

```

:::



## JAGS model estimating richness



::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: jags-mcmc-unkownR-1
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
plot(post_unknownR[,c("mu_logit_p", "mu_logit_psi", "R")])
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: jags-mcmc-unkownR-2
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
plot(post_unknownR[,c("sd_logit_p", "sd_logit_psi")])
```
:::

:::


::: {.content-card}
Mixing can be improved by focusing on a list of actual species that could have been present in the study area. 
:::



## Additional community parameters

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}
We can use the $z$ matrix to estimate additional community parameters, including the [Jaccard similarity]{.key-term} index ($S_{j,j'}$), comparing any two sites ($j$ and $j'$):

<br>

::: {.fragment}
<!-- $$ -->
<!--   S_{j,j'} = \frac{\sum_i z_{ij} z_{ij'}}{\sum_i z_{ij} + \sum_i z_{ij'} - \sum_i z_{ij} z_{ij'}} -->
<!-- $$ -->

::: {.beamer-block}

$$
  S_{j,j'} = \frac{\bar{R}_{j,j'}}{R_j + R_{j'} - \bar{R}_{j,j'}}
$$

:::

where

::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}
$R_j = \sum_{i=1}^M z_{i,j}$ is species richness at site $j$ <br>
$R_j' = \sum_{i=1}^M z_{i,j'}$ is species richness at site $j'$ <br>
$\bar{R}_j,j' = \sum_{i=1}^M z_{i,j}z_{i,j'}$ is shared species richness at sites $j$ and $j'$
:::

:::

:::



## Summary

- Two-species models allow for more control over specification of interaction effects. 

::: {.fragment}
- Community models allow for inference on richness, similarity and guild effects. 
    * It is advisable to restrict the pool of potential species to a list of actual species that could occur in the study area. 
	* This will alleviate convergence issues while allowing for species-level covariate information
:::
